title: Fourier rank versus sparsity
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
formal: Does there exist a sequence of integers \(n_{j}\ge 1\) and Boolean functions \(f_{j}:\{- 1,1\}^{n_{j}}\to \{- 1,1\}\) such that \(k(f_{j})\to \infty\) and \(r(f_{j})/\sqrt{k}(f_{j})\to \infty\) as \(j\to \infty\), where k is Fourier sparsity and r is Fourier rank over \(F_{2}\)? Equivalently, is the ratio \(r(f)/\sqrt{k}(f)\) unbounded over all finite-dimensional Boolean functions?
context:
Fourier sparsity counts the nonzero parity coefficients. Rank counts how many independent parity directions are needed to contain their support. The question asks how far these two structural measures can diverge at the square-root scale.

Sanyal’s published Theorem 1.2 gives \(r(f)=O(\sqrt{k}(f) \log (k(f)+1))\). Addressing functions attain the square-root scale up to constants. The 2021 paper explicitly asks whether that scale can be exceeded by an unbounded factor.

The 2026 linear-invariance-testing paper describes a square-root bound up to constants in a background sentence and cites Sanyal’s 2019 result. Checking that cited theorem shows that it includes log k. This citation therefore does not establish the stronger universal bound that would negatively resolve the present question.
why: Would determine whether sparse Boolean Fourier support necessarily occupies only square-root-many independent parity directions, or whether the familiar quadratic relation misses a growing separation.
status_note: Checked the 2021 question, the exact published 2019 theorem, and the 2026 property-testing paper and its cited bound. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution of the unbounded-ratio question. The 2026 background wording is not treated as a new rank theorem.

progress.text: The published upper bound is \(O(\sqrt{k} \log  k)\), within a logarithmic factor of addressing examples.
The source explicitly asks whether \(r=\omega (\sqrt{k})\) occurs for any family of Boolean functions.
A later property-testing paper cites the 2019 dimension bound in its background; checking the cited theorem preserves the logarithmic gap.

importance.reason: Asks for the exact qualitative relation between two fundamental Boolean Fourier complexity measures. Existing score retained.

sentences: A Boolean function has a Fourier expansion in parity characters.
Its sparsity counts nonzero coefficients, while its rank is the \(F_{2}\) dimension spanned by their index sets.
The question asks whether rank can exceed the square root of sparsity by an unbounded factor.
Known addressing examples attain the square-root scale, and the published universal upper bound allows an additional logarithmic factor.
The answer requires either an asymptotically separating family or a universal square-root bound with an absolute constant.

definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) and \(S\subseteq [n]\), put \(\chi _{S}(x)=\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}\), with \(\chi _{\varnothing}=1\). The Fourier coefficient is \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum _{x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}}f(x)\chi _{S}(x)\), so \(f=\sum _{S\subseteq [n]}\hat\{f\}(S)\chi _{S}\). The support is \(\operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})=\{S:\hat\{f\}(S)\ne 0\}\), and \(k(f)=|\operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})|\). It is at least one. Identify a subset S with its incidence vector in \(F_{2}^{n}\) and define \(r(f)=\dim _{F_{2}}\) span\(\{1_{S}:S\in \operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})\}\). The empty set contributes the zero vector; it may count towards k but never increases r. This rank is not a real linear-span dimension of functions. The limit \(r(f_{j})=\omega (\sqrt{k}(f_{j}))\) means that for every real \(M>0\), the ratio eventually exceeds M. No bound on \(n_{j}\) in terms of j, explicit construction algorithm, or computational efficiency is requested. The negation is the existence of a universal constant C such that \(r(f)\le C\sqrt{k}(f)\) for every n and every such f. Since \(r(f)\le k(f)\), unbounded ratios necessarily require unbounded sparsities.
answer_criterion: A positive answer must prove the existence of functions with unbounded \(r(f)/\sqrt{k}(f)\), equivalently a sequence with the displayed limits. A negative answer must prove a universal constant-factor square-root bound for every Boolean function. A fixed larger constant, finitely many examples, or a bound retaining a growing logarithmic factor does not decide the question.
